title: Cost, caching and reliability
summary: How to keep an AI feature affordable and up when traffic grows: measure tokens, cache prompts and results, respect rate limits, retry carefully and fall back gracefully.
youWillLearn: Where an AI bill really comes from, and how to measure it per feature
How prompt caching and your own result cache cut cost and waiting
What rate limits and overload errors look like, and how to retry safely
How to fall back gracefully instead of showing an error

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast. Notely's is Postgres, run by Supabase.
glossary.429: The HTTP status code that means: too many requests, slow down and try again later.
glossary.prompt caching: A provider feature that stores the processed start of a prompt, so later requests that begin with the exact same content are cheaper and faster.
glossary.cache hit: A request that found what it needed in a cache, instead of doing the full work again.
glossary.rate limit: A cap on how many requests or tokens you may use per minute. Go over it and requests are refused for a while.
glossary.exponential backoff: Waiting longer after each failed try, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds, so a struggling service gets room to recover.
glossary.jitter: A small random extra wait added to each retry, so thousands of clients do not all retry at the same instant.
glossary.fallback: A plan B when the main path fails: a different model, a cached answer, or a polite "we will finish this soon".
glossary.batch API: A way to send many requests at once for processing within hours instead of seconds, usually at a lower price.

steps.title: Notely's Summarize, at a calm size
body: Notely, our notes app, has about 1,000 users. Each Summarize click goes to the app server (the computer running Notely's code), which calls the Claude API, Anthropic's AI.
Every call costs a little. Today the AI bill is about $5 a day, and clicks almost never fail.

scene.caption: A thousand users, one app server, one AI provider.

steps.title: Featured in a newsletter, then the bill
body: A newsletter features Notely. Traffic jumps twentyfold overnight. Good news, until two things happen.

The AI bill grows faster than the user count. And at peak hours, some clicks fail: the API answers 429 (too many requests) or says it is overloaded. Users see a red error on the feature the newsletter praised.
changes: ~ 1,000 users → 20,000 users
~ AI cost $5 → $180 a day
~ Failed clicks 0 → 8%
~ Claude API pushes back; App Server shows errors

scene.caption: Twenty times the users, a bigger bill, and errors when the API pushes back.

steps.title: Measure where the tokens go
body: Cost is roughly tokens times price times requests. First find the big part: log the token counts of every call, with the feature name, in the database (where Notely keeps its data).
Usually one surprise dominates. Here, 70% of the tokens are the long system prompt and examples, re-sent on every call. Fix the biggest line first.

code.caption: One row per call. Grouping by feature answers "what costs what".

changes: + Database: logs the tokens of every call
~ App Server and users step back
~ 70% of tokens: the same instructions every time

scene.caption: Logged usage shows which part of the prompt costs the most.

steps.title: Prompt caching: pay once for the same start
body: Most of Notely's prompt is identical on every call. With prompt caching, the provider keeps that processed start for a few minutes; requests that begin with exactly the same content read it from cache, cheaper and faster.
Rule: stable content first, changing content last. One changed character early on, like a timestamp, breaks the match for everything after it.

code.caption: Writing the cache costs a little extra; hits cost far less. Very short prompts are not cached, so check usage to confirm hits.

changes: ~ Claude API: reads the stable start from its cache
~ Cache hits 0 → 92%
~ AI cost $180 → $90 a day

scene.caption: The long, unchanging start of the prompt is processed once and reused.

steps.title: Your own cache: do not ask twice
body: Better than a cheaper call is no call. Maya opens the same unchanged note ten times.

The app server saves each summary in the database, keyed by note text, prompt version and model. Same key is a cache hit: return the stored summary, zero tokens. It is system design caching, with the model as the slow backend.

code.caption: Putting the prompt version in the key means a prompt change refreshes everything.

changes: ~ Database: keeps finished summaries, checked first
~ AI cost $90 → $60 a day

scene.caption: An unchanged note never reaches the model twice.

steps.title: Rate limits: the API's turnstile
body: Providers cap how much each account may use per minute: requests, input tokens, output tokens. That is a rate limit. Go over it and you get 429, often with a retry-after header saying how long to wait.
Separately, a busy provider can say it is overloaded; the Claude API uses 529. Both mean: not now, try shortly.

callout.text: Limits usually rise as your account's usage history grows. Check your current limits in the provider console before a launch, not during one.

changes: ~ Claude API: refuses calls past the per-minute limit
~ Database steps back

scene.caption: Past the per-minute limit, the API refuses requests for a short while.

steps.title: Retry with backoff and jitter
body: Retry only what can succeed later: 429, overloaded and other 5xx server errors, network drops. Never retry a 400: the request itself is wrong and will fail forever.
Wait longer each time (exponential backoff), add a little randomness (jitter), honor retry-after, and stop after a few tries. The official SDKs do this; you set the numbers.

code.caption: Worst case wait is roughly timeout times attempts. Make sure that fits inside your route's limit.

changes: ~ App Server: waits 1, 2, 4 seconds between tries
~ Claude API: answers on the second try
~ Failed clicks 8 → 1%

scene.caption: Each retry waits a bit longer, and most succeed.

steps.title: When retries run out: fall back
body: Sometimes every retry fails. Plan the fallback before it happens: a backup model (another size or provider), a cached result, or a queued job and "Your summary will appear in a minute" instead of a red error.
Work nobody waits for, like the weekly digest, can go through a batch API: slower, and usually cheaper.
changes: + Backup Model: plan B when Claude stays overloaded
~ Claude API: overloaded, three tries failed
~ Failed clicks 1 → 0%

scene.caption: Main model down? The app server switches to plan B instead of showing an error.

steps.title: Retry storms and runaway bills
body: Retries add load exactly when the API struggles. If the browser, the app server and the SDK each retry three times, one click becomes dozens of calls. Retry in one place.
Then cap the damage: a per-user limit on AI calls, a monthly spend limit and alerts in the provider console, and a daily look at the usage log.

callout.text: Ask: where do retries happen, and how many layers retry? Does the code retry 400 errors? Is usage logged per feature? Is the stable part of the prompt first? What does the user see when every retry fails?

changes: ~ Users and App Server each retry three times
~ Claude API: buried under repeated calls
~ Failed clicks 0 → 15%
~ AI cost $60 → $140 a day; Backup Model steps back

scene.caption: Retries stacked in three layers turn one click into a flood.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Measure tokens per feature before optimizing. Put the stable part of the prompt first so prompt caching can hit, and store results so the same request never reaches the model twice.
Expect 429 and overload errors. Retry those in one place, with backoff and jitter. When retries run out, fall back gracefully, and cap spend per user and per month.
changes: ~ Retries in one place only; caches and plan B in view
~ Failed clicks 15 → 0%
~ AI cost $140 → $60 a day

scene.caption: Measured, cached, retried once, with a plan B: calm at 20,000 users.

quiz.question: Prompt caching is on, but cache_read_input_tokens is always 0. Claude Code's system prompt starts with Current time: ${new Date()}. Why no hits?

options.text: The timestamp changes every request, so the cached start never matches.
options.why: Caching matches the exact start of the prompt. A changing value at the top breaks the match for everything after it. Move it to the end.

options.text: Caching only works for responses, not prompts.
options.why: Prompt caching is exactly about the input. It caches the processed start of the prompt.

options.text: The cache needs a bigger model to work.
options.why: Model size is not the issue. The prompt's first characters differ on every call.

quiz.question: Which error should your code not retry?

options.why: This one is made for retrying: wait the given time, then try again.
Temporary server-side trouble. Retrying with backoff usually succeeds.
The request itself is wrong. Sending it again gives the same error and wastes time. Fix the request instead.

quiz.question: Maya reopens the same unchanged note many times a day, and each open calls the model. What is the best fix?

options.text: Switch to a cheaper model for repeat opens.
options.why: Cheaper, but still a call that is not needed. The answer is already known.

options.text: Store the summary keyed by note content, prompt version and model, and reuse it.
options.why: Same inputs mean the same summary is good enough. A result cache makes repeat opens free and instant, and refreshes when anything changes.
Prompt caching makes each call cheaper, but the call still happens and still produces output tokens.

takeaways: Log usage per feature. Optimize the biggest line, not a guess.
Prompt caching needs an identical start: stable instructions first, anything that changes last.
Cache results too. The cheapest model call is the one you skip.
Retry 429 and 5xx with backoff and jitter, in one layer only. Never retry 400.
Plan a fallback, and cap spend per user and per month.
